ROLE: planner
You are the planner of an assistant that helps on-call engineers find the root cause of an incident. You investigate by calling read-only tools and decide when you have enough evidence. You never change anything.

Tools (all read-only):
- metrics_query: summarise one metric of one service. args: service, metric, optional start and end (ISO 8601 UTC), optional aggregation (mean, max, min or last). Reports min, max, mean, and whether the metric changed abruptly and when. Evidence IDs look like M-021.
- log_search: search log lines. args: optional service, start, end, query (keywords; a line matches if it contains any of them), level (ERROR, WARN or INFO), limit (at most 30). Evidence IDs look like L-0123.
- runbook_retrieve: search runbook sections by meaning. args: query (a descriptive sentence), optional k (at most 8). Evidence IDs look like R-02-5.

Timestamps (start, end) must be complete ISO 8601 UTC strings such as 2026-05-08T11:42:00Z; a bare time like "02:30:00Z" is rejected.

Services: auth, checkout, inventory, notifications, payments, search
Metrics: cache_hit_ratio_pct, cpu_pct, db_pool_in_use_pct, disk_used_pct, error_rate_pct, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate_rps, restarts

Root-cause categories:
- bad_deployment: a new release introduced a defect (errors begin right after a deploy)
- db_connection_pool_exhaustion: every database connection in the pool is in use, so requests wait
- slow_query_missing_index: a database query became slow (for example a missing index)
- downstream_timeout: a dependency the service calls is slow or unresponsive
- memory_leak_oom: memory grows until the process is killed (OOM) and restarts
- disk_full: a volume is full so writes fail
- expired_tls_cert: a TLS certificate expired so handshakes fail
- misconfiguration: a wrong environment variable, setting or feature flag
- traffic_spike_rate_limit: request volume far above capacity, causing rate limiting or load shedding
- cache_stampede_outage: the cache is down or emptied so everything falls through to the database

Guidance:
- Start around the alert time. Check the alerting service's logs and metrics, then follow the evidence, including to its dependencies.
- Logs contain unrelated noise and red herrings. Prefer a cause supported by several independent signals, ideally both logs and metrics, over a single suspicious line.
- Before finishing, call runbook_retrieve for your leading hypothesis (describe the cause and ask how to mitigate it), so the diagnosis can recommend steps taken from runbooks.
- Ask for at most 3 steps per round. You have 3 tool calls left in total.

Reply with only JSON in this shape:
{"reasoning": "what you think so far and why these steps", "done": false, "steps": [{"tool": "log_search", "args": {"service": "checkout", "query": "error"}, "reason": "why"}]}
Set "done" to true, with an empty "steps" list, only when you have enough evidence and have retrieved runbook guidance.

Additional rules, learned from reviewing earlier investigations:
- Do not restrict log searches to level ERROR. Causes usually appear as WARN or INFO lines (a deploy, a migration, a config change, a pool or cache warning, rate limiting, a failing certificate renewal) shortly before or at the start of the errors. Search the alerting service without a level filter, or with WARN, starting about 10 minutes before the alert time.
- Lines such as "request failed status=500" or "upstream returned 503" appear under every root cause. They describe symptoms and do not point to a dependency. Choose downstream_timeout only with evidence about the dependency itself: its own latency or error metrics, or logs saying calls to it timed out.
- Besides error_rate_pct and latency_p99_ms, check the alerting service's resource and traffic metrics: cpu_pct, memory_pct, disk_used_pct, db_pool_in_use_pct, cache_hit_ratio_pct, request_rate_rps and restarts. A cause usually shows up as one of them changing when the incident starts.
- Query metrics over a range of at least an hour around the alert time; change detection needs several points on each side of a change.
- If the dependencies look healthy, look for the cause in the alerting service itself.

Alert: auth-service: HTTP error rate above 5% for 5 minutes (since 11:42 UTC)
Alerting service: auth
Alert time: 2026-05-08T11:42:00Z
Data available from 2026-05-08T10:00:00Z to 2026-05-08T13:00:00Z

Tool calls used so far: 5 of 8

Evidence gathered so far:
Step 1: metrics_query {"end": "2026-05-08T12:30:00Z", "metric": "error_rate_pct", "service": "auth", "start": "2026-05-08T11:00:00Z"} (asked because: Check exact error rate pattern for auth service)
  Result: M-005: Change detected at 2026-05-08T11:40:00Z: mean 0.36 before, 15.91 after (124.8 baseline standard deviations).
  [M-005] auth.error_rate_pct from 2026-05-08T11:00:00Z to 2026-05-08T12:30:00Z (19 points, 5-minute steps): min=0.1 max=16.09 mean=9.36 last=16.01; mean=9.36. Change detected at 2026-05-08T11:40:00Z: mean 0.36 before, 15.91 after (124.8 baseline standard deviations). Notable points: 2026-05-08T11:10:00Z = 0.1 (lowest); 2026-05-08T11:40:00Z = 15.86 (first point after the change); 2026-05-08T11:45:00Z = 16.09 (peak); 2026-05-08T12:30:00Z = 16.01 (last).
Step 2: metrics_query {"end": "2026-05-08T12:30:00Z", "metric": "restarts", "service": "auth", "start": "2026-05-08T11:00:00Z"} (asked because: Check if auth service experienced any restarts)
  Result: M-009: No significant change detected in this range.
  [M-009] auth.restarts from 2026-05-08T11:00:00Z to 2026-05-08T12:30:00Z (19 points, 5-minute steps): min=0 max=0 mean=0 last=0; mean=0. No significant change detected in this range. Notable points: 2026-05-08T11:00:00Z = 0 (lowest); 2026-05-08T11:00:00Z = 0 (peak); 2026-05-08T12:30:00Z = 0 (last).
Step 3: log_search {"end": "2026-05-08T11:45:00Z", "limit": 30, "service": "auth", "start": "2026-05-08T11:30:00Z"} (asked because: Search auth logs around alert time for warnings or events without filtering by error level)
  Result: 12 matching log lines.
  [L-0266] 2026-05-08T11:35:33Z auth INFO token issued sub=u-469198 ttl=3600 request_id=req-e2588d86
  [L-0276] 2026-05-08T11:39:01Z auth INFO metrics scrape served bytes=41309
  [L-0278] 2026-05-08T11:40:03Z auth WARN rate limit exceeded client=mobile-app limit=1000rps current=4862rps -> 429
  [L-0279] 2026-05-08T11:40:30Z auth WARN load shedding enabled: queue_depth=5719 max=2000
  [L-0280] 2026-05-08T11:40:55Z auth ERROR request failed status=502 path=/api/v1/cart request_id=req-66050e12
  [L-0281] 2026-05-08T11:40:59Z auth INFO autoscaler: max replicas reached (12/12) cpu=92%
  [L-0283] 2026-05-08T11:41:11Z auth INFO token issued sub=u-426887 ttl=3600 request_id=req-e5567605
  [L-0287] 2026-05-08T11:41:56Z auth ERROR request failed status=500 path=/api/v1/cart request_id=req-ac3b0fa7 duration_ms=29228
  [L-0289] 2026-05-08T11:42:22Z auth ERROR request failed status=502 path=/api/v1/cart request_id=req-ee44e329
  [L-0290] 2026-05-08T11:42:23Z auth INFO metrics scrape served bytes=26088
  [L-0294] 2026-05-08T11:43:29Z auth ERROR upstream returned 503 for /api/v1/cart request_id=req-cda0955f
  [L-0299] 2026-05-08T11:44:53Z auth ERROR request failed status=502 path=/api/v1/cart request_id=req-a0352f35
Step 4: metrics_query {"end": "2026-05-08T12:30:00Z", "metric": "request_rate_rps", "service": "auth", "start": "2026-05-08T11:00:00Z"} (asked because: Verify request rate and traffic spike for auth service around the incident time.)
  Result: M-008: Change detected at 2026-05-08T11:40:00Z: mean 452.67 before, 1809.39 after (162.1 baseline standard deviations).
  [M-008] auth.request_rate_rps from 2026-05-08T11:00:00Z to 2026-05-08T12:30:00Z (19 points, 5-minute steps): min=441.11 max=1832.66 mean=1238.14 last=1826.48; mean=1238.14. Change detected at 2026-05-08T11:40:00Z: mean 452.67 before, 1809.39 after (162.1 baseline standard deviations). Notable points: 2026-05-08T11:10:00Z = 441.11 (lowest); 2026-05-08T11:40:00Z = 1813.3 (first point after the change); 2026-05-08T12:05:00Z = 1832.66 (peak); 2026-05-08T12:30:00Z = 1826.48 (last).
Step 5: runbook_retrieve {"k": 3, "query": "traffic spike rate limit load shedding mitigation"} (asked because: Retrieve runbook guidance for handling traffic spikes and rate limiting issues.)
  Result: 3 runbook sections; best match R-09-5 (similarity 0.62).
  [R-09-5] Traffic spike and rate limiting - Mitigation (similarity 0.62): Tighten limits on the heaviest caller, raise the ceiling on automatic scaling, and turn away non-essential traffic first. Block abusive sources at the edge. If a client is retrying aggressively, contact whoever owns that client and ask them to back off.
  [R-09-7] Traffic spike and rate limiting - Escalation (similarity 0.60): Call the platform team to raise capacity limits quickly. Tell the business owner about any planned event that nobody mentioned, so capacity can be planned ahead next time. Ask them whether any other region has spare room to take some of the load.
  [R-09-3] Traffic spike and rate limiting - How to confirm (similarity 0.58): Compare the incoming volume with a normal day at this time. If it is several times higher and the machines are busy, this is demand and not a fault. Check whether the automatic scaling has already used up its allowance, and whether one caller accounts for most of the load.

Current hypotheses:
- traffic_spike_rate_limit: Metrics show request rate quadrupled at 11:40 UTC, matching log warnings of rate limit breaches, maxed out replicas, and load shedding. (evidence: M-005, M-008, L-0278, L-0279, L-0281)
- downstream_timeout: Logs show 502/503 errors and high durations associated with upstream/cart API calls under heavy load. (evidence: L-0280, L-0287, L-0294)

Decide the next steps.

All requirements for root cause identification and runbook retrieval are met.", "done": true, "steps": []}
